nameStory: The mud amnicola gets its name from its preferred habitat – the muddy bottoms of freshwater areas. 'Amnicola' comes from the Latin words 'amnis' meaning river and 'cola' meaning dweller, so this little snail is literally a 'river dweller' that loves muddy spots.
description: The mud amnicola is a tiny freshwater snail that you'd need to look very closely to spot. These miniature gastropods have small, spiral shells and belong to the duskysnail family. They're aquatic creatures that spend their lives underwater, crawling along muddy lake and stream bottoms. Like other operculate snails, they have a little door (called an operculum) that can seal shut to protect them inside their shell.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small – you'll need to look very carefully or use a magnifying glass to see details of these tiny snails

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Spiral shell that coils upward in a cone-like pattern, smooth to the touch when you can handle one

idTips.label: Operculum
idTips.description: Has a small door-like structure that can close off the shell opening – look for this round, flat piece

idTips.label: Habitat location
idTips.description: Found on muddy substrates underwater – sift through soft, silty bottom material in shallow areas

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Crawls slowly along the bottom, leaving tiny trails in soft sediment as it moves

habitat: Look for mud amnicolas in the soft, muddy bottoms of freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can burrow and feed on organic matter. You're most likely to find them in shallow water areas where the bottom feels soft and silty under your feet.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm up, easier to spot as they move around more on the muddy bottom. Look for them in shallow areas as ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're feeding and reproducing. Best time to search for them in warm, shallow water areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as temperatures drop. May burrow deeper into mud as weather cools.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, buried in bottom sediments. Very difficult to find during ice-covered periods.

funFact: Despite being one of the smallest snails you'll encounter, mud amnicolas are incredibly rare to observe in New England – they've only been officially documented three times in the entire region, making any sighting a truly special discovery!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny freshwater snails, but the combination of muddy habitat preference and the operculum (door-like shell closure) helps distinguish it. Remember: if it's tiny, in mud, and has a little door, you might have found something special.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'operculate' refers to snails that have an operculum – essentially a built-in door for their shell. This is different from many land snails that seal their shells with dried mucus. The duskysnail family name comes from their typically dark or dusky-colored shells.
compareHints: Since this is the only Amnicola species documented in our New England dataset, compare it to other small freshwater snails in the region. Unlike many other tiny aquatic snails, mud amnicolas specifically prefer muddy substrates rather than rocky or sandy bottoms. The operculum also distinguishes them from many other small freshwater gastropods that lack this shell door.
